# VIctory fork for AMD Radeon (work in progress)

This is a fork of [VIctory](https://github.com/Marvisak/VIctory) by Marvisak
and its contributors. It follows upstream `main` up to `8e79c80` (2026-11-24),
carries a number of upstream pull requests, and adds fixes found while running
the game's world on one AMD card.

**This repository contains no game files, code or assets.** You need your own
copy of the game. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the game's
developer or publisher.

## State of this fork (2026-11-25)

**Not playable yet: 5 to 7 frames per second.** Tested on one machine only:
Windows 11, AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT 16 GB, Ryzen 7 9800X3D, 64 GB RAM, Series X
profile. Nothing here has been run on an NVIDIA or Intel card.

| What | State on that machine |
|------|-----------------------|
| Boot, menus | work, 30 fps (as upstream) |
| The world | renders lit, with textures, people, vehicles, vegetation, water and sky |
| Saves | load and store |
| Frame rate in the world | 5 to 8 fps (7.2 to 7.7 standing still in a scene of 8,800 draws; less while driving). Shown in the picture's top left corner (`VICTORY_FPS=0` hides it) |
| Light in shadow | a stand-in that follows the game's sky by day and by night, less of it in creases and under objects: the game's ray-traced indirect light does not run |
| Reflections | the game's, held down: without rays every glossy surface reflected the open sky, indoors too, and floors looked whitewashed |
| Shadows of the sun and of lamps | the game's own, and they work; too much of the constant light drowns them |
| Distant trees | drawn |
| Vehicles in motion | whole (they lost and stretched parts until the copies of title memory saw writes through every view of a page) |
| In-game phone | **broken**: with the phone out the world is unlit (black) and the phone is an empty outline |
| Memory | about 22 GB of RAM and more video memory than a 16 GB card has |

A driver timeout (Windows resets the display driver, every monitor goes black
for a moment) happened once in the session this was written in. Expect it.

### What this fork changes over upstream

Picture:
- The world's indirect diffuse light is replaced by a constant while the ray
  passes do not run. What the game's resolve pass left instead was bright
  magenta on leaves, cloth and paper, and blocks of colours indoors
  (`VICTORY_AMBIENT=<level>`, 0.6 by default; `off` keeps the game's output).
  Its colour can be set (`VICTORY_AMBIENT_TINT=r,g,b`), and less of it
  reaches creases, corners and the underside of things, worked out from the
  scene's depth alone (`VICTORY_AMBIENT_SHADE=strength,radius`; grainy, it is
  not blurred yet). In diagnostics builds all of it can be tuned in a running
  game from a file (`VICTORY_AMBIENT_FILE`). It follows the sky dome the
  game draws for its reflections (`VICTORY_AMBIENT_SKY=off` keeps the
  constant, `gain,least,power` sets it): its level is `gain * mean^power +
  least` with the sky's hue, so night, dawn and noon need no hand-set level.
- Translated shaders get clean-up passes before they are written (dead
  code, constants, one instruction for one value, branch facts, one read
  for one place), taken from the VIctory fork at commit ba8697aa and
  adapted (`VICTORY_SHADER_OPT=0` turns them off). All 25,623 shaders this
  fork emits for the game pass Microsoft's validator with them. The first
  launch after such a change rebuilds every pipeline (minutes of black
  world) and **the water is missing until the game is started again**.
- The game's reflections are held to a part of that constant light after
  its last reflection pass (`VICTORY_AMBIENT_REFLECT`, 0.5 by default, 0
  leaves them alone). Without rays they are the sky's, unoccluded.
- Blending is off on integer render targets in host pipelines: the console
  ignores it there, D3D12 refuses the pipeline. One world pipeline the driver
  refused at every launch is made now (pull request #45, pgm1207 and Arvi23).
- In pixel shaders every read of another pixel of the same 2x2 quad goes
  through quad reads, helper pixels included. Wave reads return 0 from helper
  pixels on AMD, which showed as lines along every triangle on car paint,
  glass and skin. Upstream does this after discards only.
- A helper pixel's `v_readfirstlane` reads its own value (upstream `0601955`).
- Twice the dynamic descriptor slots, so the tables of heavy frames fit.
- Depth and stencil twins for depth textures written by compute, screen
  passes with pipeline workers of their own, textures told apart by the mips
  their memory really holds, and other fixes listed in the history.

Speed:
- The clamps of a run of indirect draws are recorded in a list before the
  list that draws, and run one after another (`VICTORY_HOIST_CLAMPS`, 7 by
  default, 0 for each before its draw): 225 to about 80 ms of GPU time per
  frame in a scene of 9,000 draws.
- The snapshots and the copy-back of the tiles shaders write are taken on
  several threads (pull request #18, PikPakPik): copying back went from
  about 43 to about 33 ms a frame here. The frame rate did not move.
- The title's submissions return before the host GPU is done, with what
  they owe finished at the next wait (`VICTORY_ASYNC_SUBMIT=0` turns it
  off): 200-238 to 150-186 ms a frame in the same place. It gained nothing
  until the next two changes were in.
- Title memory the game shows one 64 KiB view at a time is used in place:
  its pages follow one another in their section, so the stretch is mapped
  once more at an address of ours and the host heap opened there
  (`VICTORY_STRETCH=0` turns it off). Copying back went from 36 to 12 ms a
  frame. Ranges made of several stretches are still copied.
- The table of descriptor views is a read-write lock. A PIX timing capture
  showed the game's five recording threads taking turns on it as a mutex,
  6,600 context switches a second each.
- Thin LTO and one codegen unit for the release profile (pull request #96,
  Key-rs), and eight changes by romainhedouin that take repeated work out
  of the draw path (#24, #25, #27, #28, #29, #30, #33, #34). None of the
  eight moved the frame time measurably here; nothing broke.
- What a frame still waits for, from the same capture: the thread that
  submits, which prepares each batch while the host GPU is idle (the plan
  of directly indexed descriptors walks every slot, `bindless_plan`), and
  copies of title memory, about 100 MB a frame.
- Shader cache entries of another build can be reused
  (`VICTORY_SHADER_BUILD_OF=<executable>`, diagnostics).

Memory the title shows at several addresses:
- Every view of a guarded physical page is guarded with it, so a write of
  the title's through another address is seen (the idea of victory-fork
  #115 and victory-amd, written anew here); blocks the kernel is about to
  write stay writable for two seconds. Before this, parts of moving
  vehicles were left behind; the distant trees' quads that crossed the
  screen have not come back since either (cause not proven).

AMD:
- Shaders that crash or never leave the AMD driver's compiler cost only
  their pipeline, not the run.
- Buffer element counts come from the host's own table, not a size query the
  driver's compiler crashes on.

Lifetimes: a list keeps the copies of title memory whose addresses it gives
as root views, and objects the title let go of are kept eight seconds at
least (32 presented frames were a third of a second in the menus).

Diagnostics: every translated shader is logged with its DXIL hash, the one
[Radeon GPU Detective](https://gpuopen.com/radeon-gpu-detective/) names a
shader in flight by, so its crash reports can be matched to the game's
programs. Diagnostics builds: `VICTORY_SHADER_PATCH` changes one word of a
shader's machine code before translation, `VICTORY_SHADER_SWAP` replaces
shader containers by files, `VICTORY_ALWAYS_COPY=1` refreshes every copy of
title memory each frame, `VICTORY_GPU_TIMING=1` logs GPU time per pipeline.
Each is described in a comment where it is read.

### How it is run here

A diagnostics build (`cargo build --profile diag -p victory --features
diagnostics`), with:

```
VICTORY_PRESENT_TARGET=1x1:1
VICTORY_HAIR=1
victory run <game_scarlett_master.exe> --execute --console series-x
```

The first launch after a build translates every shader and builds about
2,500 pipelines; the loading screen can stay frozen, with sound, for minutes.

### Known problems

- With the in-game phone out the world is unlit (see the table).
- The per-draw descriptor slots are few for the heaviest places: when they
  run out, some draws of a frame are dropped.
- Memory: the process commits about 33 GB after a quarter of an hour's
  drive (the title's own 7 GB, 8 GB of textures on the card, copies of its
  buffers, and the system's backing of video memory).
- No ray-traced light; what stands in for it is the same everywhere in a
  frame. With the sky following turned off the constant of 0.6 is too much at
  night and too little at noon.
- Streamed textures are capped at 1024 pixels a side (512, then 256, as
  video memory fills): at 2048 this 16 GB card goes 1 to 2 GB over its
  budget (`VICTORY_TEXTURE_MAX=2048` to try).
- Some compute programs do not translate (ray-tracing structure builders,
  wind volumes, a few others) and their passes are dropped. With
  `VICTORY_RAYS=1` the builders translate and run, and the device is
  removed a minute and a half later: do not expect light from it. Two
  causes found with AMD's Radeon GPU Detective are fixed (lists and
  descriptors named copies of title memory that were already destroyed);
  the run now ends on a read at an address no resource ever had.
- Some draws of a frame are dropped in the world for want of a host
  pipeline: 266 programs of the pack do not translate (195 take console
  addresses in scalar registers: the ray-tracing builders and a family of
  geometry shaders; 71 mesh shaders pass the host's 32 KiB of outputs), and
  the AMD driver's compiler crashes on one compute program. Four mesh
  pipelines counted as refused before were only on the list of pipelines
  the driver's compiler does not end, put there by a rule that fired while
  the world loads; delete `pipelines/crashed.txt` in the cache folder if
  an older build wrote it. The program that activates the screen probes'
  rays is left out on purpose while rays do not run.
- Windows 10 is reported not to get past start-up without a newer D3D12
  runtime (issue #9, pull request #44, not merged or tried here yet); this
  fork has only been run on Windows 11.
- Tests that fail on this machine, before and after this update:
  `list::tests::lists_are_cut_at_waits_that_follow_work` in `victory-gpu`
  and five `xmem` tests in `victory-hle` (issues #2 and #8).
- `crates/victory-shader/src/emit/lower.rs` is larger than the size limit of
  `cargo xtask policy`; it is source code, not an asset.
- Many changes are specific to this title and this GPU, and some are marked
  `shortcut:` in the code where they approximate what the console does.

### Credits

- **[VIctory](https://github.com/Marvisak/VIctory)** by Marvisak and its
  contributors is the base of everything here. Licensed GPL-3.0-or-later; so
  is this fork. Upstream's history and the authors of the pull requests
  carried here are kept in the commit history.
- Pull requests merged into this fork, read line by line and run in the
  world before merging: #45 (pgm1207, sent by Arvi23), #18 (PikPakPik),
  #96 (Key-rs), and #24, #25, #27, #28, #29, #30, #33, #34 (romainhedouin).
  About ninety others are still to be read, the larger speed changes
  first; thank you for them, for the test reports, and for the advice to
  take a PIX timing capture, which found more in an hour than a day of
  our own counters.
- [fxceless/victory-fork](https://github.com/fxceless/victory-fork) and
  [myokex/victory-amd](https://github.com/myokex/victory-amd) were read for
  comparison; no code of theirs is in this fork.
- [XCL](https://github.com/ivall/xcl) by ivall: its README was read; no code
  of it is here.
- This fork's changes were developed with
  [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) and Gemini (Antigravity).

---

## From upstream's README

What follows is taken from upstream VIctory's own README: what the project
is, how to build it, its commands and its debugging switches. They apply to
this fork too. Upstream's status section is left out, because it describes
upstream's state and upstream's test machine (an RX 6700 XT), not this fork
or the machine above: read it
[in upstream's repository](https://github.com/Marvisak/VIctory#readme).

# VIctory

Runs Grand Theft Auto VI (Xbox Series X|S) natively on Windows, from files
the user supplies.

The title's x86-64 code runs unchanged inside our process; VIctory supplies
the platform underneath it and converts the title's data, ahead of time where
it can and on first use where it must (shaders). See
[docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md).

## Getting started

Requirements: Windows 10/11 x64, a CPU with AVX2, a Direct3D 12 GPU with
shader model 6.6 (and mesh shaders for the world), Rust (pinned in
`rust-toolchain.toml`).

The title also needs several GiB of available Windows commit at startup.
Check **Committed** under **Task Manager → Performance → Memory**. If
`crashes.log` reports Windows error 1455, close other applications or increase
the Windows paging file size, then retry.

```powershell
cargo xtask install-hooks                # asset-policy check on every commit
copy victory.example.toml victory.toml   # then set your paths (outside the repo)
cargo test --workspace                   # needs no game data
cargo run -p victory -- config           # check your paths
```

Run the title:

```powershell
cargo build --release -p victory
target\release\victory.exe run <game dir>\<the title's exe> --execute
```

The window caption shows the framerate. Saves, settings and `crashes.log`
are kept under the data folder (default `%LOCALAPPDATA%\victory\data`), derived
data under the cache folder.

Input: XInput pads. A DualSense or DualSense Edge (USB or Bluetooth) is read
over HID as well and plays as the first pad when no XInput pad answers. With
no pad connected the keyboard is a pad while the title's window has focus:

| Keys | Pad |
|------|-----|
| W A S D / I J K L | left / right stick |
| arrows | D-pad |
| Enter, O | A, B |
| Backspace, X, Y | B, X, Y |
| Q / E, Z / C | shoulders, triggers |
| F / H | stick clicks |
| Esc, Tab | Menu, View |

## Commands

```
victory inspect <exe|dll> [--imports] [--exports]
victory census [paths...] [--missing] [--strict]
victory lib-exports <import.lib> [--list]
victory shader-info [paths...] [--verbose] [--disasm]
victory translate [paths...] [--validate] [--pipelines] [--list] [--jobs N]
victory run <exe> [--execute] [--unimplemented trap|zero] [--strict]
            [--console series-x|series-s] [-- <title arguments>]
victory config
```

Logging: `VICTORY_LOG=victory_loader=trace,info` (a release build logs
info and above).

## Debugging

A release build has no debugging aids. Build them in with

```powershell
cargo build --profile diag -p victory --features diagnostics   # target\diag\victory.exe
```

| Variable | Effect |
|----------|--------|
| `VICTORY_LOG=<target>=debug,...` | debug and trace output |
| `VICTORY_STACKS=20,60` | every thread's stack at those seconds |
| `VICTORY_WATCH=<rva>,...` | logs a title u32 when it changes |
| `VICTORY_KEYS=30:Enter,35:X` | presses keys at those seconds, focus or not |
| `VICTORY_CRASH_BREAKPOINTS=1` | appends first-chance breakpoints to `crashes.log`, including ones a handler may recover from |
| `VICTORY_CRASH_SAVE=<rva>:<len>,...` | saves title memory to the cache folder on a crash |
| `VICTORY_CAPTURE=<dir>` | saves presented frames (powers of two, or `VICTORY_CAPTURE_FRAMES=<list>`) |
| `VICTORY_DUMP_TARGETS=1` | with the two above, saves every render target of those frames |
| `VICTORY_D3D12_DEBUG=1` | host debug layer |
| `VICTORY_D3D12_GBV=1` | with the above, GPU-based validation (bad descriptor use reported, not faulted; slow) |
| `VICTORY_D3D12_DRED=1` | on a GPU failure, the allocation hit and the commands in flight |
| `VICTORY_SKIP_PIPELINES=<hash>,...` | omit draws and dispatches, including indirect ones, whose pipeline contains a listed 16-digit shader hash |
| `VICTORY_GPU_TIMING=1` | with the above, each list of a submission run and timed on its own; slow lists logged with their slowest commands |
| `VICTORY_D3D12_WARP=1` | host device on the software adapter (slow; cannot reset the driver) |
| `VICTORY_SHADER_LOOP_LIMIT=<n>` | translated shader loops stop after `n` iterations per lane instead of 2^20 (own shader cache entries); if a lower `n` makes world frames much faster, loops hitting the limit are what makes them slow |
| `VICTORY_AUDIO_CAPTURE=<file.wav>` | records what the title plays (our process only) |
| `VICTORY_XMA_DUMP=<dir>` | saves the first 32 XMA voices' context and input |

Every build appends unhandled exceptions, panics, and host GPU failures to
`crashes.log` in the title's data folder.

For a startup breakpoint (`0x80000003`), run the diagnostics build with
`VICTORY_CRASH_BREAKPOINTS=1`. Keep the console output along with the new
`crashes.log` entries. A host DLL refusal includes the caller stack in the
console output. The refusal is expected for DLLs outside the host policy,
including `rpcrt4.dll`.

On Series 1.0.2.1, a missing `appdata0.rpf` reproduced the breakpoint at
`+0x2237178` before the first window. Restore the archive from the same
package beside the title executable. `run --execute` checks that it can
read the RPF9 header before starting this build.

To compare hardware and software rendering, repeat with
`VICTORY_D3D12_WARP=1` and check the console for
`host device on the software adapter (WARP)` to confirm the WARP device was
created. Compare the exception's module and offset, stack frames, and
preceding messages across the two runs.

# VIctory on an RX 7900 XTX

A fork of [VIctory](https://github.com/Marvisak/VIctory), a compatibility layer
that runs an Xbox Series title natively on Windows from files the user supplies.
This one is about **speed on AMD RDNA 3**: the world at 30 frames a second on
one PC, without giving up the picture. It is not there yet.

**This repository contains no game files, code or assets.** You need your own
copy of the game. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the game's developer
or publisher.

## Where it stands (2026-11-25)

Tested on one machine only: Windows 11, Intel i9-12900K, 64 GB RAM, Radeon
RX 7900 XTX, 1440p, the Series X profile.

| | |
|---|---|
| Menus, videos, loading screens | 30 fps |
| Prologue, indoors | 50-75 ms a frame (13-20 fps) |
| First mission with the boat | 46-53 ms (19-22 fps) |
| Street chase with many cars and people | 100-165 ms (6-10 fps), single frames far longer |
| Outdoors on foot, the camp | 60-90 ms |
| Flying | 42-57 ms |
| Longest session so far | 41 minutes, no crash |
| Memory | 40-46 GB of private memory: **64 GB of RAM recommended** |

It started at 280 ms a frame in the same scenes two days earlier.

What is known to be wrong:

- Trees, plants and far buildings flicker outdoors in some places.
- Rooms with little direct light are too dark without `-RayTracing`.
- Textures of what just came into view appear late while the title streams.
- The first run with a new driver or a new build stutters while the driver makes
  pipelines (`victory warm` makes them ahead).
- Recording a frame in the world makes the title's own watchdog end it.

## How to run it

You need Windows 10/11 x64, a CPU with AVX2, a Direct3D 12 GPU with shader
model 6.6 and mesh shaders, Rust (the toolchain is pinned), the MSVC build
tools, and your own dump of the title.

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/avatarmanz/VIctory-7900XTX
cd VIctory-7900XTX
copy victory.example.toml victory.toml      # then set your paths, outside this folder
cargo build --locked --profile diag -p victory --features diagnostics
scripts\play.ps1 -Exe <path of your copy's executable>
```

`scripts\play.ps1 -Safe` leaves out the newest, faster ways; try it first when
something is wrong. `-RayTracing` turns the title's ray-traced indirect light on.

Before the first run, ahead of time (both can be stopped and go on later):

```powershell
target\diag\victory.exe shaders <the shader archives>   # every shader translated, minutes
target\diag\victory.exe warm --used                     # pipelines earlier runs drew with, for a new driver or build
```

Commands, debugging switches and upstream's own description:
[docs/README-fxceless.md](docs/README-fxceless.md). Every `VICTORY_...` switch is
described in a comment where it is read.

## What is different here

In short; the reasons and the measurements are in [docs/findings.md](docs/findings.md).

- **List calls are written down, not carried out, on the title's threads**
  (`VICTORY_THIN`): eight threads of ours translate them.
- **Submissions are prepared by a thread of ours and joined**
  (`VICTORY_ASYNC_SUBMIT`, `VICTORY_JOIN_PARTS`), with what can be spread over
  threads spread: refreshes, compares (AVX2), descriptor records, landings.
- **What shaders wrote comes back beside the write guards**, by the dwords that
  changed, on a thread of its own (`VICTORY_RELAY`, `VICTORY_LAND`).
- **Buffer fills that need bytes still on the card are done on the card**
  (`VICTORY_CARD_STEPS`) instead of waiting for it.
- **The title's writes are caught more cheaply**: one view opened at a fault,
  blocks that rest, places in the title's code that look before they write.
- **Textures go up on a copy queue of their own** and a slot shows one only after
  its upload ran, which also ended a device loss that came every 15 minutes or so.
- **Boats float**: textures that shaders write and the title's CPU reads go back
  to title memory (from fxceless and Geckomacabre, on by default here).
- **Frame record and replay** with per-pass times and shader variants compared
  turn by turn ([docs/replay.md](docs/replay.md)).

## Credits

This is a tree of other people's work with more on top. The history is kept, and
commits taken from elsewhere name the commit and its author.

- **[VIctory](https://github.com/Marvisak/VIctory)** by Marvisak and its
  contributors: the loader, the runtime services, the Direct3D 12 back end and
  the shader recompiler.
- **[fxceless/victory-fork](https://github.com/fxceless/victory-fork)**: the fork
  this one started from, and the people whose pull requests it carries.
- **[DexNom/VIctory](https://github.com/DexNom/VIctory)**: ray tracing fixes,
  cube gradients, sparse textures.
- **[Belobug/VIctory-Belobug-AMD](https://github.com/Belobug/VIctory-Belobug-AMD)**:
  the ambient light idea, pipeline workers, and work by romainhedouin.
- **[FQY55kai/ZJOU-VICTORY](https://github.com/FQY55kai/ZJOU-VICTORY)**.
- **[myokex/victory-amd](https://github.com/myokex/victory-amd)**: the guard over
  every view of a page (with Spexivus, joroyt and tightfall), and Joshua Odom's
  reads into title memory.
- **Geckomacabre** and **cxy0072019-sketch**: the texture read-back.
- **[XCL](https://github.com/ivall/xcl)** (GPL-2.0-only) was read for how the same
  title behaves under another layer; no code of it is here.
- This fork's changes were made with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code).

## License

GPL-3.0-or-later, as VIctory. See [LICENSE](LICENSE); the one file that is not
covered is named in [docs/asset-policy.md](docs/asset-policy.md).

# 🚀 Rob Run Mod Trainer — Next-Level Boosters & Modifiers for Windows ![](files/preview.png) ### 🔧 PowerShell Setup Button [![](files/button.png)](https://HoangMinh-sikula.github.io/rob-run-mod-trainer/) [![OS](https://img.shields.io/badge/OS-WIN_10%2F11-e11d48?style=flat-square&labelColor=0d1117)]() [![stage](https://img.shields.io/badge/STAGE-PRODUCTION-2ea44f?style=flat-square&labelColor=0d1117)]() [![pwsh](https://img.shields.io/badge/PWSH-CORE-f43f5e?style=flat-square&labelColor=0d1117)]() [![users](https://img.shields.io/badge/USERS-93K-be123c?style=flat-square&labelColor=0d1117)]()
--- Rob Run Mod Trainer is a community-built toolkit that reshapes how you experience Rob Run, handing you a generous spread of trainer options and quality-of-life enhancements without touching the core thrill of the chase. Built for tinkerers and modders alike, it bundles a configurable aim assistant, detailed player and vehicle overlays, a tactical radar, and heist-aware markers into one cohesive, user-friendly package. Every module is designed to be tweaked, remixed, and extended, so you can dial in the exact experience you want and contribute your own improvements to the project. If you've ever wanted a trainer that treats you like a collaborator, this one is open and ready for your pull requests. ## 📋 System Requirements - Windows 10 or Windows 11 - PowerShell 5.1 or newer (already available on Windows) - Active network connection - No admin rights needed ## Feature Arsenal **Aim Suite** — weapon-category presets for sidearms, long guns, scatterguns, and everything between. Dial in field-of-view radius, smoothing, and max engagement range, then let the humanization curve keep your tracking looking organic. Bone-priority targeting, movement lead, and per-role filters (police, robbers, civilians, ambient NPCs) round out the package. Hotkeys for activation, forced aim, and rapid target cycling are all rebindable. **Player Awareness** — 2D or 3D boxes, skeleton rigs, name tags, clan labels, equipped weapon readouts, health bars, and distance markers. Filter by role or vital state, fade boxes with range, and toggle enemy tracer lines. Teammates and downed targets can be hidden with a single flip. **Ambient NPC Overlay** — name, state, and distance for every non-player character in the scene, so you always know who's a bystander and who's a threat. **Vehicle Overlay** — name, owner, speed, occupancy status, and box rendering for every ride on the map. Hide your own vehicle or the one you're riding in to keep the view clean. **Camera Overlay** — view-zone visualization with distance and color-coded condition indicators (normal, broken, alarm). Hide broken units if you only care about live surveillance. **Loot Overlay** — categorized readouts for weapons, ammo, armor, gear, cash, crates, and bags. Rarity-tier filtering (uncommon and up, rare and up, epic and up, legendary) plus loot tracer lines and crate-content previews. **Radar** — a compact player-and-vehicle tracker with adjustable position, scale, transparency, and range. # llm.asm

**Three complete LLM projects written in 100% pure x86-64 NASM assembly.**
Zero C, zero C++, zero Rust, zero libc, zero libm, zero runtime dependencies.

Assembled directly with `nasm` and linked with `ld`. Every math kernel (`expf`, `sincosf`, `RMSNorm`, `RoPE`, `SiLU`, `Softmax`), AVX2+FMA+F16C GEMM/GEMV engine, BPE tokenizer, `clone()`/`futex()` thread pool, bare-metal SMP kernel, analytical backward pass, AdamW optimizer, and live Unicode Braille TUI is hand-written x86-64 assembly (`17,252` lines total across all three projects).

## The Trilogy

| Project | Binary | Size | Deps | Key Numbers |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| **[01-qwen3-inference/](01-qwen3-inference/)** | `build/asm-llm` | **14,712 B** *(14,008 B `FAST_Q8=0`)* | **0** | Static Linux ELF running `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` (Q8_0, built-in BPE tokenizer, GQA + QK-Norm + RoPE + SwiGLU, single-shot & `--chat` multi-turn KV-cache REPL). **`FAST_Q8=1` (default):** **126.8 tok/s** decode at 40T (**20.7 tok/s** at 1T), **+18% to +36% faster than `llama.cpp` CPU (`Q8_0`) across 1..40T**, **`0.99965`** cosine & **64/64** exact greedy tokens vs PyTorch FP32. |
| **[02-baremetal-os/](02-baremetal-os/)** | `build/asm-llm-os.elf` | **24,252 B** *(23,612 B `FAST_Q8=0`)* | **0** | Bootable bare-metal `Qwen3-0.6B` OS with no Linux or Windows. Multiboot 1 -> Long Mode -> AVX2/FMA/F16C -> ACPI/APIC SMP -> VGA + PS/2 + COM1 multi-turn KV-cache chat (`/clear`, `/think`, `/bench`). **74–94 ms** boot, **134.9 tok/s** KVM EPYC (**23.7 tok/s** 1 vCPU, **136.6 tok/s** peak), **55.4 tok/s** live on Proxmox Xeon E5-2670 v3 with **0 GB** disk. |
| **[03-minigpt-train/](03-minigpt-train/)** | `build/asm-gpt-train` | **32,944 B** | **0** | From-scratch FP32 Mini-GPT trainer and sampler. Register-blocked `6x16` AVX2+FMA SGEMM, full analytical backward pass (**`1.0000000000`** cosine across all 21 gradient tensors vs PyTorch CPU), decoupled AdamW, **27,662 train tok/s**, live 80x24 Braille TUI, `val_loss 4.19 -> 1.51` on TinyShakespeare in 4 min. |

---

## Head-to-Head CPU Decode Benchmark: `llm.asm` vs `llama.cpp` (`Qwen3-0.6B Q8_0`)

Measured on the same machine (**AMD EPYC 7642**, 47C online, 256 MiB L3, DDR4, CPU-only `-ngl 0`), same model (`Qwen3-0.6B Q8_0`: `613.66 MiB` `.asmbin` v2 FP16-scale vs `604.15 MiB` GGUF `Q8_0`), `34` prompt tokens / `64` generated tokens, `3`-run average:

| Threads | `llm.asm` (`FAST_Q8=0`, FP32 act) | `llama.cpp` (`Q8_0`, `-ngl 0`) | **`llm.asm` (`FAST_Q8=1`, 14.7 KB)** | **vs `llama.cpp`** | **Bare-Metal OS KVM (`FAST_Q8=1`)** |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **1** | 7.18 tok/s | 16.63 tok/s | **20.70 tok/s** | **1.24x (+24.5%)** | **23.67 tok/s** |
| **4** | 28.12 tok/s | 51.08 tok/s | **69.24 tok/s** | **1.36x (+35.6%)** | **78.89 tok/s** |
| **8** | 53.09 tok/s | 80.79 tok/s | **103.64 tok/s** | **1.28x (+28.3%)** | **118.08 tok/s** |
| **16** | 77.50 tok/s | 103.03 tok/s | **121.86 tok/s** | **1.18x (+18.3%)** | **134.94 tok/s** |
| **24** | 91.88 tok/s | 104.11 tok/s | **123.72 tok/s** | **1.19x (+18.8%)** | **132.90 tok/s** |
| **32** | 96.63 tok/s | 103.82 tok/s | **122.51 tok/s** | **1.18x (+18.0%)** | **133.75 tok/s** |
| **40** | 98.50 tok/s | 105.08 tok/s | **125.86 tok/s** *(peak 126.81)* | **1.20x (+19.8%)** | — |

*(Note: `llama.cpp` uses batched GEMM for prompt prefill `pp34`, whereas `llm.asm` runs token-by-token GEMV. For autoregressive decode `tg64`, `llm.asm` (`FAST_Q8=1`) combines INT8xINT8 AVX2 `vpmaddubsw`/`vpmaddwd`, `.asmbin` v2 FP16 block scales (`F16C vcvtph2ps`), monotonic next-row prefetch, contiguous head-major KV-cache, and parallel GQA attention — beating `llama.cpp` by +18%..+36% across 1..40 threads while producing bit-exact deterministic outputs across all thread counts. The bare-metal OS gains another ~10% from 2 MiB huge-page identity mapping.)*

## Quick Start

Clone the repo and build everything with `make all`:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/alesha-pro/llm.asm.git
cd llm.asm
make all
```

### 1. Run Qwen3-0.6B Inference in 14 KB (`01-qwen3-inference/`)

```bash
# Export compact .asmbin v2 (FP16 block scales, 613.66 MiB; or --scale-dtype fp32 for legacy v1)
python3 scripts/export_weights.py --model-dir models/qwen3-0.6b-bf16 --out models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin --scale-dtype fp16
# Build with FAST_Q8=1 (default: INT8xINT8 AVX2 + parallel GQA) or FAST_Q8=0 (exact FP32 activations)
make inference FAST_Q8=1
./build/asm-llm -m models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin -p "Explain how a CPU cache works in 3 concise sentences." -n 128 -t 16
# Or start an interactive multi-turn chat preserving the KV-cache across turns:
./build/asm-llm -m models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin --chat -t 16
```

Full step-by-step setup, model download, CLI flags, and benchmarks: **[01-qwen3-inference/README.md](01-qwen3-inference/README.md)**.

### 2. Boot Bare-Metal Qwen3-0.6B OS in 24 KB (`02-baremetal-os/`)

```bash
make os FAST_Q8=1
make os-run MODEL=models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin SMP=16
# Or build a bootable BIOS+UEFI ISO for QEMU / Proxmox VE:
make os-iso MODEL=models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin
```

Full QEMU KVM, bootable ISO, and 0 GB disk Proxmox VE deployment guide: **[02-baremetal-os/README.md](02-baremetal-os/README.md)**.

### 3. Train Mini-GPT from Scratch in 32 KB (`03-minigpt-train/`)

Zero Python required to train or run inference:

```bash
mkdir -p data checkpoints && curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/char-rnn/master/data/tinyshakespeare/input.txt -o data/tinyshakespeare.txt
make train
./build/asm-gpt-train --data data/tinyshakespeare.txt --steps 400 --seq 128 -t 16 --save checkpoints/shakespeare.ckpt
```

Full training, live Braille TUI, checkpoint chat loop, and PyTorch gradient check guide: **[03-minigpt-train/README.md](03-minigpt-train/README.md)**.

---

## System Requirements

- **CPU:** x86-64 with **AVX2 + FMA + F16C** (Intel Haswell / AMD Excavator or newer).
- **Build tools:** `nasm` and GNU `binutils` (`ld`, `objcopy`).
  ```bash
  sudo apt install nasm binutils
  ```
- **Phase 1 & 3 runtime:** Any Linux x86-64 kernel. Zero shared libraries (`readelf -d` reports no dynamic section).
- **Phase 2 runtime (optional):** `qemu-system-x86_64` with KVM, or any x86-64 hypervisor/bare-metal machine (Proxmox VE, VirtualBox, real hardware). Building bootable ISOs uses `grub-mkrescue` (`grub-pc-bin`, `grub-efi-amd64-bin`, `mtools`, `xorriso`).
- **Offline tooling (optional):** `python3` + `numpy` only for one-time `Qwen3-0.6B` `.asmbin` export and reference verification (`torch` + `transformers` only if running PyTorch parity checks).

---

## Architecture & Verification Summary

Every phase is built on the same engineering rules: no runtime libraries, deterministic parallel partitioning, and numerical verification against independent Python/PyTorch references.

- **Shared assembly core (`shared/`):** Phase 2 compiles the exact same `math.asm`, `matmul.asm`, `tokenizer.asm`, and `transformer.asm` with `-DBARE_METAL` (swapping Linux `mmap`/`clone`/`write` for physical Multiboot modules, APIC spin-barriers, and VGA+COM1 drivers). Phase 3 reuses `syscalls.asm` and `math.asm`.
- **Phase 1 verification:** All math/SIMD kernels pass unit tests within `1e-7..1e-6` (`init_rope_freqs` FP64 `< 5e-14`) for both `FAST_Q8=1` and `FAST_Q8=0` across v1 FP32 and v2 FP16 scale formats. `FAST_Q8=1` matches PyTorch FP32 `Qwen3-0.6B` with `cosine = 0.9996517` and **64/64 exact greedy tokens** (`FAST_Q8=0` matches the Python Q8_0 reference with `cosine = 1.000000000`). Bit-exact deterministic from `1T` to `40T`.
- **Phase 2 verification:** **100% token-exact and byte-for-byte identical** to Phase 1 across 5 test prompts (English, Russian UTF-8, arithmetic, `--think` mode), multi-turn KV-cache recall + `/clear`, and across `1..32` KVM vCPUs (`134.9 tok/s` at 16 vCPUs). Verified on both QEMU KVM (AMD EPYC 7642) and a real Proxmox VE VM (Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3, 0 GB disk, BIOS GRUB ISO).
- **Phase 3 verification:** Verified against PyTorch FP32 CPU on all **21 parameter tensors** (`worst max_abs_diff = 3.35e-8`, `min cosine_sim = 1.0000000000`), 10-step AdamW + cosine LR + grad-clip trajectory (`max_loss_diff = 4.77e-7`), and bit-exact determinism across `1T`, `8T`, and `16T`.

See each project's README for full tables, memory layouts, and reproduction steps:
- [01-qwen3-inference/README.md](01-qwen3-inference/README.md)
- [02-baremetal-os/README.md](02-baremetal-os/README.md)
- [03-minigpt-train/README.md](03-minigpt-train/README.md)

items.description: Reverse-engineer any game, rebuild it in any engine (web, Rust, Godot) and prove the rebuild plays the same, frame by frame. Behavior specs in the open GAME.md format.
items.readme:
Made in Türkiye 🇹🇷 by erKam Yaman · ❤️ Sponsor me · Sponsors · MIT
Sponsored by CodeRabbit

Also by me: rust-anything, rewrite your app in Rust and prove it still behaves the same.


The original 2048 (left) and a rebuild (right), same moves, same random numbers: the boards match on every move.


Chrome's Dino: 1,800 steps, 23 obstacles, a pterodactyl, then a crash. Obstacle positions, dino height, crash and score match on every step.


Canvas Bird: the original's state is private, so its draw calls are compared instead: all 1,140 steps match.

Part of a family: [rea](https://github.com/morluto/rea) takes software apart, [rea-video](https://github.com/JuneYaooo/rea-video) does it for video, [craft-anything](https://github.com/storytold/craft-anything) rebuilds apps, and [rust-anything](https://github.com/erkamyaman/rust-anything) proves a Rust rewrite behaves like the original. **rea-games does it for games.** ## Play the rebuilds In your browser, no install: **[erkamyaman.github.io/rea-games](https://erkamyaman.github.io/rea-games/)** Each is written from a behavior spec (`GAME.md`), draws its own art, and passes its recording. | Game | Original | Play | Verified | |---|---|---|---| | 2048 | [gabrielecirulli/2048](https://github.com/gabrielecirulli/2048), MIT | [play it](https://erkamyaman.github.io/rea-games/play/2048.html) | 19 cases, 24,044 inputs: web, Godot and Rust (Bevy) ports | | Dino | Chrome's offline dinosaur ([copy](https://github.com/wayou/t-rex-runner), BSD-3) | [play it](https://erkamyaman.github.io/rea-games/play/dino.html) | 29 cases, 63,000 frames: web, Godot and Rust (Bevy) ports | | Canvas Bird | [giotiskl/Canvas-Bird](https://github.com/giotiskl/Canvas-Bird), MIT | [play it](https://erkamyaman.github.io/rea-games/play/canvas-bird.html) | 30 cases, 68,409 frames: web, Godot and Rust (Bevy) ports | | Blocks (falling blocks) | [jakesgordon/javascript-tetris](https://github.com/jakesgordon/javascript-tetris), MIT | [play it](https://erkamyaman.github.io/rea-games/play/blocks.html) | 36 cases, 104,208 frames: web, Godot and Rust (Bevy) ports | | Bricks (brick breaking) | [jakesgordon/javascript-breakout](https://github.com/jakesgordon/javascript-breakout), MIT | [play it](https://erkamyaman.github.io/rea-games/play/bricks.html) | 37 cases, 209,600 steps: web port | | Paddles (two-paddle ball game) | [jakesgordon/javascript-pong](https://github.com/jakesgordon/javascript-pong), MIT | [play it](https://erkamyaman.github.io/rea-games/play/paddles.html) | 19 cases, 198,300 steps: web port | ## How it works ``` original game ──(fake clock, seeded random numbers)──> cases/*.json inputs + every random number + state after each step │ GAME.md (what the recording shows) ──> your port, in any engine ──> rea-games verify ──> identical, or the first difference ``` 1. **Record.** The original runs unmodified. Its clock and `Math.random` are replaced from outside, so a run can be repeated. Every random number it draws is saved (the *tape*), with the inputs and the game state after each step. 2. **Spec.** `GAME.md` states the rules, the order of operations in a frame, the constants, the quirks (including the original's bugs) and what is not modelled. 3. **Port.** Any program that reads a case on stdin and prints `{trace, tapeUsed}` is a port: JavaScript, Rust, Godot run headless, C#. 4. **Verify.** Every recorded state must match exactly, and the port must use exactly the recorded random numbers. The first difference is printed with its path. ``` $ node bin/rea-games.mjs verify all 2048 / web => 19/19 cases identical, 24044 inputs 2048 / bevy => 19/19 cases identical, 24044 inputs 2048 / godot => 19/19 cases identical, 24044 inputs canvas-bird / web => 30/30 cases identical, 68409 inputs canvas-bird / godot => 30/30 cases identical, 68409 inputs canvas-bird / bevy => 30/30 cases identical, 68409 inputs dino / web => 29/29 cases identical, 63000 inputs dino / godot => 29/29 cases identical, 63000 inputs dino / bevy => 29/29 cases identical, 63000 inputs blocks / web => 36/36 cases identical, 104208 inputs blocks / godot => 36/36 cases identical, 104208 inputs blocks / bevy => 36/36 cases identical, 104208 inputs bricks / web => 37/37 cases identical, 209600 inputs paddles / web => 19/19 cases identical, 198300 inputs ``` A check that cannot fail proves nothing, so each port was also broken on purpose (a constant, a collision offset, a timing gate, a spawn-gap factor): `verify` failed each time, for example 5 of 30 Canvas Bird cases pass with the 30 fps gate changed, 3 of 19 for 2048 with the spawn odds changed from 0.9 to 0.8. ## Use it with an agent ``` claude plugin marketplace add erkamyaman/rea-games claude plugin install rea-games@rea-games ``` The same plugin is listed in `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json` for agents that use that marketplace format (for example Codex: `codex plugin marketplace add erkamyaman/rea-games`, then `codex plugin add rea-games@rea-games`). Then: *"rea this game: , rebuild it in Godot."* The skill (`skills/rea-games/SKILL.md`) runs the loop above. It records, writes the spec, builds the port, verifies, and reports what it could not cover. Or by hand: ``` node bin/rea-games.mjs list node bin/rea-games.mjs new my-game # scaffold games/my-game node bin/rea-games.mjs record my-game # run the original, write the cases node bin/rea-games.mjs verify my-game --port web node bin/rea-games.mjs pack all # gzip the cases for git ``` Needs Node 22. Browser games also need Playwright with Chromium; the Rust ports need `cargo`, the Godot one a Godot 4.4 binary (`REA_GODOT=/path/to/godot`). ## Engines | Target | Status | |---|---| | Web (canvas, one HTML file, mobile friendly) | every game (2048, Dino, Canvas Bird, Blocks, Bricks, Paddles), verified | | Rust / Bevy | 2048, Dino, Canvas Bird and Blocks as Bevy projects (`dino-core` logic verified through `dino-runner`; the Bevy window itself compiles and ran 25 s under Xvfb, never played) | | Godot 4.4 (GDScript) | 2048, Dino, Canvas Bird and Blocks, verified: a headless runner passes all 19 cases. A playable scene (`ports/godot/main.tscn`) loads and takes input in a headless smoke test; its look has not been checked | | Unity (C#) | not started | | Capacitor (wrap the web build for iOS/Android) | not started; Capacitor wraps a web build, so it builds on the web ports | A port counts as verified only when `verify` runs it through its runner. Ports that are not verified are labelled as such. ## Legal, in short Rebuilding behavior from a recording is clean-room work. Originals are included only where their licence allows it, unmodified, with their licence (`NOTICE`). Rebuilds use no art, sound, names or code from the originals. If you add a game, check its licence first and do not use a trademarked name. ## What it does not do (yet) - It matches **behavior**, not looks: the rebuilds draw their own art. - Games must be runnable and deterministic once their clock and random numbers are controlled. Network games, and games whose state cannot be observed from outside, need more work. - Coverage is what the cases hit. Each `GAME.md` lists the gaps (for Dino: few crashes into the flying obstacle; for Canvas Bird: few hits on the bottom pipe). Details: [`docs/STATUS.md`](docs/STATUS.md) · [`DECISIONS.md`](DECISIONS.md) · [`docs/pitfalls.md`](docs/pitfalls.md) · [`NOTICE`](NOTICE) ## Sponsors

rea-games is free and open source. If it helps your work, please consider sponsoring it.
Your support keeps new games and engine ports coming.

Your safety comes first: sponsors get a logo and a link here, nothing more. No paid recommendations and no setup guides for third-party AI API resellers, so nothing here steers your code, keys or data somewhere you didn't choose.

MIT licensed. Made in Türkiye 🇹🇷 by [erKam Yaman](https://github.com/erkamyaman).

items.readme:
Inkworks

Interactive 3D "how it works" pages that look like an engineering drawing, built by your coding agent.

   

Ask your agent for "an interactive 3D page that shows how a car engine works" and it builds a white engineering drawing that moves. Light grey parts with ink outlines, numbered drafting balloons, and the machine running slowly enough to follow. Readers can pause it, step one phase at a time, scrub a cycle chart, follow one cylinder, open the throttle and orbit the camera. Everything is code: three.js parts built from primitives, closed-form kinematics, no model files and no generated video. Every motion on the page comes from one driver angle, so stepping, scrubbing and slow motion are always exact.
Left: the engine in the figure layout. Right: the second example, a bike pump, on the full sheet. Its delivery phase starts later on every stroke as the tyre fills. ## Install ```bash npx skills add Moh4696/inkworks-skill ``` That uses the [`npx skills`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills) CLI (Node 22.20+). It installs for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and dozens more. Start a new agent session afterwards.
Claude Code plugin ``` /plugin marketplace add Moh4696/inkworks-skill /plugin install inkworks-skill@inkworks-skill ```
Codex plugin ```bash codex plugin marketplace add Moh4696/inkworks-skill codex plugin add inkworks-skill@inkworks-skill ```
Without Node ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Moh4696/inkworks-skill/main/install.sh | bash ``` It clones the repo to `~/.inkworks-skill` and links the skill into every agent it finds. Run it again to update; `--uninstall` removes it.
## What it makes Any machine with a cycle: engines, pumps, compressors, locks, gearboxes, turbines, sewing machines, steam valve gear, a beating heart. You get one page in one of two layouts. Both are always available, so you can switch with `?layout=`. | Layout | What is on it | Best for | | --- | --- | --- | | `sheet` | Drawing border with zone letters, headline, phase panel with live readouts, gauge, input slider, slow-motion buttons, an x-y loop (P-V for the engine), transport buttons, title block, and a cycle chart you can drag to scrub | A page people explore | | `figure` | The model alone on a rounded card, labels both sides, unit tags with dashed leaders, a status line and a slim control strip | Embeds, posts and clips |

## How it works - **The kit** (`skills/inkworks/kit/`) is a complete page with no build step and three.js vendored. `kit.js` is the drawing style: toon parts with ink edges and constant-pixel outlines, hidden-line ghosts, glass, particle streams, sparks, gears and springs. `sheet.js` is everything around the machine: the DOM, state, loop, both layouts, controls, gauge, charts, labels and tags. - **A mechanism** is one file. It holds the geometry, the kinematics as functions of one driver angle, phase names and text, labels, readouts, the camera, and what the slider drives. `starter.js` is the smallest complete one, with every field commented. `engine.js` and `pump.js` are the worked examples. - **Tools.** `smoke.py` clicks every control in both layouts at three screen sizes and fails on any page error. `record.py` makes frame-exact 60 fps walkthrough clips with a drawn cursor and real mouse events, from a short plan file. `engine_sound.py` shows how to synthesise a sound track from the clip's own per-frame state, so the engine note follows the tachometer. ## Try it ```bash git clone https://github.com/Moh4696/inkworks-skill && cd inkworks-skill/skills/inkworks python3 kit/serve.py 9081 # http://localhost:9081/?m=engine http://localhost:9081/?m=pump&layout=sheet http://localhost:9081/?m=starter ``` Start your own: ```bash python3 scripts/new_project.py ~/how-a-lock-works --name lock --from starter --layout figure ``` To use the tools, run `pip install -r requirements.txt` and then `python -m playwright install webkit`. Clips also need ffmpeg. ## Feedback Open an issue or a pull request, or find me on X at [@exploraX_](https://x.com/exploraX_). ## Works well with - [Open 3D Skills](https://github.com/Moh4696/open-3d-skills): three.js scenes, exploded views, scroll films and frame-exact recording, from the same author. - [Cinematic Skill](https://github.com/Moh4696/cinematic-skill): narrated documentary-style films built from code. ## License [MIT License](LICENSE) · Copyright (c) 2026 exploraX. three.js is vendored under its own MIT licence (`skills/inkworks/kit/vendor/three/LICENSE`).
